Tunisia’s Electric Utilities Sector Reels Amid Mounting Debt Crisis

TUNIS, June 23 — Tunisia’s electric utilities sector is facing its most severe financial turmoil in decades as a mounting debt crisis threatens to destabilize power supply and ongoing infrastructure projects, according to industry officials and analysts.

The crisis intensified this month after two of the country’s largest power providers, Société Maghrebienne d’Électricité (SME) and Tunisie Énergie S.A., reported difficulties servicing outstanding loans totaling more than 1.2 billion dinars ($390 million). Multiple sources confirmed that local banks have sharply curtailed credit lines to utilities, citing rising concerns over loan defaults.

“The sector is under immense pressure. Access to fresh capital has virtually dried up,” said Habib Mekki, spokesperson for the Union of Electrical Workers. “Many projects to upgrade transmission lines and expand capacity have been put on hold.”

Electricity supply remains stable for residential customers, but industry insiders warned that some utilities are struggling to maintain regular payments for imported fuel and equipment. “We are at risk of not meeting our contractual obligations with suppliers,” said a senior manager at SME, speaking on condition of anonymity. “If this continues, disruptions in service could occur within weeks.”

According to figures from the Tunisian Association of Electric Utilities, total sector debt has surged by 35% since last year, driven partly by higher fuel import costs and a drop in payment collection rates. The credit freeze has left smaller regional providers especially vulnerable, with reports of delayed maintenance work in several governorates.

“The inability to refinance debt is hitting everyone from the largest firms to small cooperatives,” said Amira Ben Salah, an energy analyst based in Tunis. “We risk a situation where infrastructure deteriorates and investment collapses.”

Government officials held emergency talks with industry leaders on Thursday but offered no immediate solution. “We are aware of the gravity of the situation and are working on a financial support package,” said Hichem Abdelli, director-general at the Ministry of Energy. “However, budget constraints limit our options.”

Unions have warned of potential layoffs if the liquidity crisis is not resolved swiftly. “Our members are worried about their futures,” Mekki said. “There is real fear on the ground.”

As negotiations continue, the sector remains in a precarious position, with the debt crisis casting a long shadow over Tunisia’s electric utilities.
